summary: Describes conventions for using the SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 hash algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax, including with the Digital Signature Algorithm and ECDSA. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A hash is a short fingerprint of a file. This document says how to use the stronger members of the SHA fingerprint family in a common signing format.

questions: how to use sha-2 with cms
which hashes can be used with dsa in cms
absent or null parameters in algorithmidentifier
subtitle: Which identifiers and parameters to use when SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 appear in signed or digested CMS messages.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needed agreed identifiers and parameter rules for the SHA-2 family of hash algorithms and for signatures that use them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects the existing object identifiers for SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 and for DSA, RSA and ECDSA signatures with them, says when parameters must be absent or NULL, and gives SMIMECapabilities values.
tldr.outcome: It defines no new identifiers and adds no new security considerations. It is a Standards Track document that updates RFC 3370.

today: RFC 5754 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2010 that updates RFC 3370. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Document Covers
sections.content:
RFC 5754 specifies the algorithm identifiers and parameters for the message digest algorithms SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 when they are used with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) from RFC 5652. The digest algorithms themselves are defined in the Secure Hash Standard, with reference code in RFC 4634.

It also covers using these digests with the DSA, RSA (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5) and ECDSA signature algorithms, and it gives SMIMECapabilities attribute values for each algorithm.

The RFC creates no new identifiers. They come from RFC 3874, RFC 4055 and RFC 5758, so no ASN.1 module is included. Message authentication with HMAC and the same hashes is left to RFC 4231.
sections.eli5: Many people already invented names for these fingerprint recipes. This document does not invent new names. It gathers the right ones in one place and says how to use them in signed messages.

sections.title: The Four SHA-2 Digest Algorithms
sections.content:
Digest algorithm identifiers appear in the digestAlgorithms field of SignedData, and in the digestAlgorithm field of SignerInfo, DigestedData and AuthenticatedData. Digest values appear in the DigestedData digest field and in the Message Digest authenticated attribute, and they are also the input to signature algorithms.

Each identifier is an object identifier under the NIST hash algorithm arc: id-sha224 ends in 4, id-sha256 in 1, id-sha384 in 2 and id-sha512 in 3. Each is wrapped in the standard AlgorithmIdentifier structure, which holds an object identifier and optional parameters.
sections.eli5: Each of the four fingerprint recipes gets its own long number-name. That name goes in a box in the message so the reader knows which recipe was used.

sections.title: Absent or NULL Parameters
sections.content:
The AlgorithmIdentifier parameters field is optional. For the SHA-2 digest identifiers, implementations MUST accept absent parameters, MUST accept NULL parameters, and MUST generate absent parameters.

The RFC explains the history. Two encodings exist because the OPTIONAL marker was lost when the 1988 ASN.1 syntax for AlgorithmIdentifier was translated into the 1997 syntax. It was later restored by a defect report, but by then many people thought parameters were mandatory, so some implementations encode a NULL and others omit the field. The correct encoding is to omit it.

There is one exception. PKCS#1 (RFC 3447) requires the padding for RSA signatures to use SHA-2 identifiers with NULL parameters, so the rule to generate absent parameters does not apply to that padding.
sections.eli5: Some programs leave a blank box on the label and others write the word NULL in it. Everyone has to understand both, but when you write a new label you should leave the box empty.

sections.title: Signature Algorithms with SHA-2
sections.content:
Signature algorithm identifiers go in the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm field of SignedData, and also in the same field of countersignature attributes. The signature itself goes in the SignerInfo signature field.

DSA follows the conventions of RFC 3370 for keys and values, and MAY be used with SHA-224 and SHA-256 only. SHA-384 and SHA-512 are not supported because the maximum bit length of p (called L) is 3072 for DSA. For matching strength, SHA-384 would need L of 7680 and SHA-512 would need L of 15360. The parameters field MUST be absent.

RSA (RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5) MAY be used with all four hashes through the identifiers sha224WithRSAEncryption, sha256WithRSAEncryption, sha384WithRSAEncryption and sha512WithRSAEncryption. Here the parameters MUST be NULL, but implementations MUST accept them absent as well as present.

ECDSA follows RFC 5753 and is defined for SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 as ecdsa-with-SHA224 through ecdsa-with-SHA512. The parameters field MUST be absent.
sections.eli5: A signature is a fingerprint locked with a secret key. Each lock type works with certain fingerprint sizes, and for each pairing the label has to be written in a set way.

sections.title: SMIMECapabilities Values
sections.content:
A program can advertise what it supports with the SMIMECapabilities attribute from RFC 5751. For each algorithm the RFC gives the exact DER bytes of the SMIMECapability, which is a SEQUENCE holding the algorithm's object identifier.

For the digests, the capability uses the identifier with absent parameters; for example id-sha256 is 30 0b 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 01. The DSA and ECDSA capabilities also use absent parameters, while the RSA ones carry NULL parameters (the trailing 05 00).
sections.eli5: A program can hold up a card saying which fingerprint recipes it understands. The RFC spells out exactly what the card should look like, byte by byte.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds nothing of its own here. It says the security considerations in RFC 3370, RFC 3874, RFC 4055, RFC 5753 and RFC 5758 apply, and that no new security considerations are introduced by this specification.
sections.eli5: This document only writes down labels, so it says to read the safety notes in the documents it borrowed the labels from.
